messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

George, a 76-year-old European American man and a retired hotel manager, still lived in the same suburban town where he had run a mid-sized hotel for nearly three decades. The traumatic event had occurred three years ago, during his last year on the job. A maintenance worker had accidentally mixed two cleaning agents in the hotel’s laundry room, releasing a cloud of chloramine gas. George, who had been doing a walk-through on that floor, inhaled a lungful before the ventilation system kicked in. He was not hospitalized, but the coughing, burning sensation, and the acrid, bleach-like smell stayed with him.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of the event came back not as a coherent story but in fractured, disconnected pieces—the sudden sting in his throat, the sight of the worker’s panicked face, then nothing. Sometimes he would feel the full terror of that moment without any accompanying image, as if his body remembered even when his mind could not. And at odd moments, especially near cleaning supplies or in certain hallways, that chemical smell would return, vivid and real, triggering a surge of helplessness. He began to believe his body had betrayed him. He could no longer trust its reactions—his heart would race, his chest tighten, his throat close up—and he came to see his own body as an enemy that kept sounding alarms long after the danger had passed. These negative appraisals deepened his sense of helplessness: bad things could happen anytime, and he could do nothing to stop them.

That feeling of being at the mercy of his own body made him constantly alert. He felt on guard even inside his own home, especially when he heard unexpected or loud sounds—a car backfiring, a door slamming, a dropped pan. Those sounds would jolt him, and the sudden alertness would summon the fragmented memory pieces: the acrid smell, the burning, the worker’s face. The memory intruded on the threat, and the threat, in turn, made the memories more vivid and more frequent. He found himself only able to feel truly safe in a very limited number of places—his bedroom, a specific chair in his living room, and nowhere else. The hotel itself he now avoided entirely, even though it had been his workplace for decades; he had retired early on medical grounds. But even at home, the world outside felt dangerous.

To manage these constant threats, George developed strategies. He kept the television or music playing loudly almost all day, using sensory distraction to drown out the silence that might let a random sound startle him. He also monitored his own thoughts constantly, scanning for any sign that he might be “going crazy”—a sudden flash of fear, a stray image, a scent. When he became aware that he was alert, he would turn up the volume or retreat to his safe chair. Yet these strategies had a dark side: they reinforced the belief that his body and mind were unreliable. Every time he needed to distract himself or check his thoughts, it felt like further proof that he could not trust himself, that he remained helpless. The more he used these strategies, the more his negative appraisals strengthened, and the more on guard he felt.

A few weeks before he sought help, George was sitting in his living room when the mail truck backfired outside. The sharp crack sent him into a full panic: his chest seized, he smelled chlorine, and he spent the next hour pacing, unable to shake the feeling that something terrible was about to happen. He realized that his life had shrunk to a single chair, that he could no longer visit his daughter on the other side of town, and that even the safety of his home felt fragile. What frightened him most was the thought that his own body would never stop reacting, that he would always be a prisoner of a memory that had no clear picture but all the force of a live event. He came to therapy hoping to find a way to trust himself again, even though he was not sure that was possible.
